answer.label: Written by

answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine line from the Tao Te Ching, Chapter 33. The exact English wording — “overcomes…is strong…overcomes himself is mighty” — is James Legge’s 1891 translation. Note that the widely-shared “He who conquers others…” form swaps in “conquers” and is a later variant of Legge’s “overcomes.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Tao Te Ching (Dao De Jing), Chapter 33
James Legge, 1891 (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39)
Classical Chinese: “勝人者有力，自勝者強”

source.excerpt: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will.
trail: The line sits in Tao Te Ching, Chapter 33, a short verse on self-knowledge and self-mastery that dozens of translators have rendered.
The precise wording — “overcomes others is strong…overcomes himself is mighty” — is James Legge’s 1891 translation, verbatim.
Legge’s version appears in The Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39 (1891), long in the public domain.
The popular “conquers others…conquers himself” form is a modernized variant of Legge’s “overcomes.”
source.excerptNote: Chapter 33 in James Legge’s 1891 translation. Legge renders the Chinese 有力 (“has force”) as “strong” and 強 (“strong/firm”) as “mighty.”
source.rightsNote: The Chinese original has been in the public domain for over two millennia, and this specific English wording comes from James Legge’s 1891 translation (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39), first published well before 1931 — so it too is public domain in the United States. Modern translations of Chapter 33 (e.g. Stephen Mitchell’s 1988 “Mastering others is strength; mastering yourself is true power”) remain under copyright, but that is not the wording quoted here.

author.name: Lao Tzu
author.heading: About Lao Tzu
author.metaLine: fl. 6th century BC (traditional) · Chinese philosopher · reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Lao Tzu (“Old Master”) is the semi-legendary figure traditionally credited with founding philosophical Taoism and authoring the Tao Te Ching. Modern scholars doubt he was a single historical person and date the text to roughly the 4th–3rd centuries BC, but the work itself is very real — a foundational classic of Chinese thought on the Way (Tao), simplicity, and self-mastery. Chapter 33, from which this line is drawn, is one of its most quoted passages.

misattribution.heading: Wording watch
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Lao Tzu is correct — this really is Tao Te Ching, Chapter 33. The catch is the wording: the internet circulates several forms, and the most popular one is not what Legge actually wrote.

items.who: “He who conquers others is strong; he who conquers himself is mighty”
items.why: This “conquers” form is the most-shared version (see Goodreads), but Legge’s 1891 text reads “overcomes,” not “conquers.” The swap is a later smoothing.

items.who: “Mastering others is strength; mastering yourself is true power”
items.why: A popular alternative that is Stephen Mitchell’s 1988 rendering, not Legge’s — same verse, different (in-copyright) translation.

misattribution.truthLine: All these forms trace to the same genuine source — Tao Te Ching, Chapter 33 — but the exact quoted wording (“overcomes…mighty”) is specifically James Legge’s 1891 translation.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Chapter 33 builds a ladder of paired virtues: knowing others is intelligence, but knowing yourself is wisdom; overcoming others is strength, but overcoming yourself is might. The point is that the harder, more valuable conquest is inward.

The line has stayed popular for the same reason it was written — it reframes power. External dominance looks impressive; mastering one’s own impulses is the rarer and, in Lao Tzu’s framing, the greater achievement.
